blocks.instruction: Read the following passage and answer the questions.
blocks.passage:
People often describe attention as though it were a lamp that simply illuminates whatever stands before the mind. The metaphor is useful, but it can also mislead. A lamp does not decide where to shine, whereas attention is continuously guided by expectation. When readers approach a paragraph, they do not process every mark with equal weight. They predict which ideas will matter, test those predictions against the next sentence, and revise them when the text resists an easy interpretation. What feels like passive reception is therefore an active cycle of selection and correction.

This cycle explains why background knowledge can improve comprehension without guaranteeing it. Prior knowledge supplies useful expectations, allowing a reader to connect details quickly and to recognize the likely purpose of an example. Yet the same expectations can become a trap. A familiar phrase may encourage the reader to supply a conclusion that the author never makes. Skilled reading requires a balance: predictions must be strong enough to organize the text but flexible enough to be abandoned. Evidence from the passage, rather than familiarity alone, must decide whether an interpretation survives.

The balance becomes especially important when a writer introduces contrast. Words such as however, instead, and nevertheless do more than join sentences. They signal that an earlier expectation is about to be restricted or replaced. A reader who notices only the vocabulary of individual sentences may understand each local claim and still miss the direction of the argument. By treating contrast markers as instructions for updating a mental model, the reader can preserve both speed and accuracy. The goal is not to predict less. It is to predict provisionally and to revise without reluctance.

For this reason, effective annotation should record relationships rather than decorate every difficult word. A brief note such as old view, limitation, or new claim often captures more of the argument than a long list of definitions. The best annotation is not the one containing the most ink; it is the one that makes the author's sequence of expectations visible when the reader looks back.

These habits can be practiced deliberately. Before reading, a student may turn a heading into a tentative question. During reading, the student can mark the sentence that changes the direction of the discussion. Afterward, a short summary can compare the initial prediction with the author's actual conclusion. None of these steps requires extensive notes. Their value lies in making revision visible, so that a mistaken expectation becomes evidence of learning rather than a reason to continue defending the first interpretation.
